title: The ROI of AI: Why you need Eval Framework - Beyang Liu
talk_summary: Beyang Liu (Sourcegraph CTO) argues that measuring AI ROI reduces to measuring developer productivity, which is intractable, so he presents six pragmatic evaluation frameworks customers use (headcount, A/B velocity, time-saved-from-engagement, KPIs, OKR impact, surveys). The talk is mostly about selling/justifying AI tools to finance, not about engineering techniques for running agents.

takeaways.technique: Define explicit success criteria per initiative before adopting a tool
takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of generic metrics (lines of code), customers pick specific KPIs tied to desired org changes (e.g., more time on features/tests/review, less time answering questions) and evaluate against those.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Define clear success criteria um that's something that both you your internal teams and stakeholders will appreciate

takeaways.technique: Lower-bound time-saved accounting from engagement events
takeaways.what_they_do: Tag each product action (search, chat, inline generation) with a conservative time-saved estimate, sum a lower bound, and compare against hourly cost to justify spend.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you can lower bound it and just say like okay we're going to get a lower bound estimate on the total amount time saved
takeaways.numbers: Developer hour valued ~$1,200; tool ~$9/month; 'a couple minutes a month' pays for itself

takeaways.technique: Prefer one strong lever over many mediocre parallel workers
takeaways.what_they_do: Invokes Mythical Man-Month: one highly productive engineer beats many mediocre ones needing guidance; asks whether you want 100 mediocre AI devs or a 100x lever for strong humans.
takeaways.evidence_quote: do you want 100 mediocre AI developers or do you want a 100x lever for uh the human developers

takeaways.technique: Graduate autonomy: inline assist -> interactive agent -> offline automation
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues reliability comes from moving along the autonomy spectrum incrementally rather than jumping to fully automated offline agents, keeping human feedback in the loop at intermediate stages.
takeaways.evidence_quote: not jumping straight to the full automation because that's a very difficult problem
